what_it_does: Modern processors leak information through indirect, timing-based side channels — for example, an attacker can infer a program's secrets by watching how long certain memory-cache operations take, or by observing the side effects of speculative execution (where the processor runs instructions ahead of time as a guess). Existing defenses tend to patch one attack type at a time, leaving systems exposed to other variants. This paper proposes a processor design that tries to address the problem broadly: at runtime, each instruction is decoded into either a 'secure' version (designed to leave no timing traces) or a faster 'performance' version, depending on whether the data being handled is considered sensitive. The idea is that non-sensitive code runs at full speed, while sensitive code is automatically shielded. The approach is prototyped on RISC-V BOOM, an open-source out-of-order processor design, though the abstract does not detail how data sensitivity is determined or what the performance cost is.
